This article aims at an in-depth analysis of the relation of certain activities and services in daily life to the growth of climate change. Climate change is one of the most characteristic occurrences of the modern world, if not the most. It is a byproduct of the greenhouse effect, which is a natural phenomenon necessary for sustaining life on the planet. However, human activities have heavily contributed to the rise of an unbalanced amount of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, causing the anthropogenic aspect of climate change. Despite the doubts on the human influence on climate change, there is indisputable scientific proof to verify it. The consequences of climate change appear to be very severe, both for the environment and humans themselves, while they are expected to escalate in the future. It is widely known that the industrial revolution is the landmark of anthropogenic climate change. But despite the industry’s influence being common knowledge, what are the everyday actions of each individual or household that are key contributors to the phenomenon? 

 Transportation is one of the most harmful everyday activities, especially aviation due to emissions from the combustion of fossil fuels used to power the vehicles. Surprisingly, the food industry is also a sector very high in emissions, mostly due to emissions from livestock production. Another cause is deforestation stemming from multiple factors, a very important one being paper production. While trees absorb carbon dioxide, when cut, they emit it back into the atmosphere, resulting in further emissions. Especially damaging is water overuse, due to the disruption of the water cycle. Furthermore, the burning of fossil fuels for general use (e.g. heating) and specifically for electricity is a big contributor in greenhouse emissions. Certain gardening activities can also contribute in the emissions. Lastly, waste is very damaging to the atmosphere. The decomposition of waste is responsible for emitting significant quantities of CO2 and methane. The need to combat climate change is very pressuring. While individual changes in lifestyle are very vital, bigger changes need to be implemented in order to effectively mitigate climate change.

The article examines in depth how certain everyday activities and services relate to the growth of climate change. Climate change is among the defining phenomena of the modern world, if not the most prominent. It results from the greenhouse effect, a natural process essential to sustaining life on Earth. Yet human activities have greatly increased the imbalance of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, giving rise to the anthropogenic dimension of climate change. Although some question human influence, there is undeniable scientific evidence confirming it. Its effects are expected to become even more severe in the future and are already profoundly harmful to both the environment and people. The industrial revolution is widely regarded as the turning point for anthropogenic climate change. However, beyond the well-known impact of industry, which everyday actions by individuals and households are major drivers of the phenomenon?

Transportation is one of the most damaging daily activities, especially aviation, because of emissions from burning fossil fuels to power vehicles. The food industry is also highly emissions-intensive, largely because of livestock production. Deforestation is another major cause, arising from several factors, with paper production being an important one. Trees absorb carbon dioxide, but when they are cut down, that carbon is released back into the atmosphere, adding to emissions. Water overuse is especially harmful because it disrupts the water cycle. In addition, burning fossil fuels for general purposes such as heating, and specifically for electricity, is a major source of greenhouse emissions. Some gardening activities can also add to emissions. Finally, waste is very damaging to the atmosphere: as it decomposes, it releases significant amounts of CO<sub>2 </sub>and methane. The need to fight climate change is urgent. While individual lifestyle changes are important, larger-scale measures are necessary to effectively mitigate it.
